# Larkholm Island Council: ferry renewal briefing note

This is a fictional briefing note written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Background

The island's only ferry, the diesel vessel MV Gannet, is 27 years old. Its maintenance bill has risen every year since 2021, and the operating contract with the Larkholm Ferry Company ends in 2028.

## Usage

Council counts show 412,000 one-way crossings in 2025. Of these, 61% took place between June and September.

## Options before the Council

Option 1 is a diesel refit costing $3.1 million, which would extend the vessel's life by about eight years. Option 2 is a battery-electric replacement costing $14.2 million. The national Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel's cost if the Council commits before 30 September.

## Council constraints

The Finance Committee will not raise the annual ferry subsidy above $1.8 million. Any decision to buy a new vessel needs evidence of sustained use and a funding plan before the March budget vote. Councillors from the harbour ward have said they will not back a plan that cuts winter service for islanders.

## Timeline and open questions

The grant deadline is 30 September. Grid upgrades for charging at both terminals are expected to take 14 to 18 months, and the diesel vessel would keep running throughout. Officers have not yet agreed how the cost of the charging upgrades would be shared. The operator has proposed a fare increase to cover part of that cost; the Council has not taken a position on the size of any increase.

# Larkholm Ferry Company: electric ferry feasibility memo

This is a fictional memo written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Ridership

Our ticketing system recorded 365,000 one-way crossings in 2025. About 58% of them were between June and September.

## What an electric ferry would change

A battery-electric vessel would cut fuel use and operating emissions on the route by about 90% and save roughly $0.9 million a year in fuel. Charging at both terminals needs grid upgrades that will take 14 to 18 months, so the diesel vessel must keep sailing until they are finished.

## Our proposal

To protect the battery and leave time for charging, we propose a reduced winter timetable of four daily return sailings from November to March, instead of today's six. We also propose a 12% fare increase to help pay for the charging equipment.

## Risks we want the Council to understand

Battery vessels have less power in reserve in heavy weather, so more winter sailings may be cancelled in storms. If the grant deadline is missed, the electric option is unlikely to be affordable. We do not yet know how many islanders will accept fewer winter sailings, and we have not surveyed them.

documents.name: 03-residents-survey-summary.md
documents.content:
# Larkholm Residents' Association: ferry survey summary

This is a fictional survey summary written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Who answered

The Association surveyed 1,150 islander households and received replies from 52% of them.

## What islanders said

68% of respondents ranked year-round reliability above emissions reductions. 71% oppose a reduced winter timetable, and 64% oppose a 12% fare increase. 52% said they would support an electric ferry if six sailings a day were kept in winter.

## Who depends on the ferry in winter

The Larkholm Health Centre reports about 140 patient trips a month to mainland clinics between November and March, including dialysis appointments that cannot be rescheduled. Many nurses, teachers and shift workers commute by the first and last sailings of the day.

## What the Association asks

The Association asks the Council to guarantee at least six winter sailings a day and to cap any fare increase at 5%. It will not oppose an electric ferry that meets these two conditions.

documents.name: 04-stakeholder-statements.md
documents.content:
# Stakeholder statements on the ferry proposal

This is a fictional collection of statements written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Green Tide Alliance

The Alliance polled 400 visitors and residents and found that 74% support an electric ferry. The Alliance states that islanders overwhelmingly prefer the electric ferry even with fewer winter sailings. It estimates that the diesel ferry emits about 2,900 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and urges the Council to accept the Clean Coasts Fund grant before 30 September. It proposes paying for winter service from summer fares.

## Harbour Business Council

Visitors account for about 70% of summer crossings, and summer visitor spending is worth around $9.5 million a year to island shops, guest houses and cafes. The Business Council supports an electric ferry because it would strengthen the island's green image. It warns that any fare increase above 5% would reduce day-trip bookings and asks that construction never disrupt the June to September season. It wants eight summer sailings a day.

documents.content:
# Scenario assumptions (analyst-provided)

This is a fictional set of planning assumptions written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. They are inputs chosen by the analyst, not facts from any source.

- A1. The Council commits to the electric ferry before the grant deadline, so the Clean Coasts Fund pays 40% of the vessel cost.
- A2. Fares rise by 12% when the electric ferry enters service.
- A3. From November to March the timetable is cut from six to four daily return sailings.
- A4. Charging works finish about 16 months after the decision, and the diesel vessel keeps sailing until then.
- A5. No new subsidy is available beyond the current $1.8 million ceiling.
- A6. Stakeholders learn about decisions through a broadcast notice board that everyone sees and through smaller topic communities where like-minded people talk.

These assumptions frame the what-if question. They are not predictions, and the simulation does not test whether they are realistic.

sections.title: Community Support Trends Over Six Discussion Rounds
sections.body:
The fictional Larkholm community engaged in a six-round scenario simulation to evaluate responses to replacing the island’s aging diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel, including a proposed reduced winter timetable from six to four daily return sailings and a 12% fare increase.

Initially, opinion was moderately supportive (around 15% average), but over the rounds, there was a marked and steady shift toward overwhelming approval (final average about 92%), with unanimous support and zero active opposition by round 6. The overall polarization decreased substantially, reflecting rising consensus. This shift coincided with a critical intervention in round 4 where the Council assumed a guarantee to maintain six daily winter sailings and cap fare increases at 5%, addressing key community and stakeholder concerns.

Residents valued year-round ferry reliability far above emissions reductions; a fictional survey found 68% prioritized winter reliability, 71% opposed reducing winter sailings, and 64% opposed a 12% fare rise, with only 52% supporting the electric ferry if six winter sailings were kept (S5). The Health Centre reported significant monthly patient travel during winter months, emphasizing the necessity of stable winter connectivity (S5). The Council’s constraints included a maximum annual subsidy ceiling and political opposition from harbor ward councillors to any cut in winter service (S1, S2).

The electric ferry would slash operating emissions by about 90% and save roughly $900,000 annually in fuel costs (S3). However, risks were noted regarding reduced winter sailing power reserves potentially causing more cancellations in storms and the delayed infrastructure upgrades (14-18 months) required for charging, meaning diesel service would continue meanwhile (S3).

Stakeholders represented diverse interests:
- The Green Tide Alliance strongly supported the electric ferry, emphasizing its vital emissions reductions and backing the council’s guarantee both for winter sailings and fare caps, proposing summer fares subsidize winter service to sustain connectivity (S6, M-plaza-2-agent-4, M-plaza-4-agent-4, M-community-6-agent-4).
- The Harbour Business Council supported the ferry for environmental and branding benefits but stressed limiting fare increases to under 5% to protect visitor numbers and summer tourism revenue (~$9.5M annually) and insisted on maintaining six winter sailings to support off-season economic activity (S6, M-plaza-6-agent-5).
- Community representatives voiced concerns about fare affordability and winter reliability, strongly advocating the Council guarantee six winter daily return trips and a fare rise cap of 5% to protect local residents’ needs and health-related journeys (S5, M-community-1-agent-3, M-community-4-agent-1).
- The Ferry Company CEO confirmed commitment to the electric ferry transition aligned with maintaining diesel service during charging infrastructure upgrades and highlighted the necessity of community engagement to foster trust amid the timetable adjustments (M-plaza-5-agent-2).

The simulated discourse produced a broad alignment: residents and community proxies accepted the electric ferry conditional on retaining winter service at six daily crossings and limiting fare increases to 5%. Stakeholders balanced the climate benefits (90% emissions reduction) and annual fuel savings ($0.9M) against operational risks and community needs.

Critical enablers of support were transparent communication about service changes, clearly guaranteed winter timetable maintenance, and controlled fares to avoid socioeconomic exclusion. Uncertainties remain regarding winter period power reserve risks and infrastructure cost sharing, but the scenario reveals a plausible pathway for Larkholm to simultaneously advance environmental sustainability while safeguarding essential year-round connectivity and economic vitality.

Overall, the fictional Larkholm scenario demonstrated how a battery-electric ferry replacement, combined with a reduced but guaranteed winter timetable and moderated fares, can gain near-unanimous support by addressing both environmental goals and core community concerns.

sections.title: Economic and Environmental Considerations
sections.body:
The fictional stakeholders on Larkholm exhibit a strong and increasing support for replacing the island ferry with a battery-electric vessel, conditional on maintaining vital winter service levels and limiting fare increases. Initial opinions were mixed with moderate support averaging around 15%, but through six rounds of simulated discussion, consensus overwhelmingly shifted to roughly 92% support with unanimous backing by the final round and minimal opposition across community and plaza platforms. This consensus emerged as stakeholders balanced environmental, economic, and social factors.

Key benefits recognized by all parties include a drastic reduction of operating emissions by approximately 90% and annual fuel savings close to $0.9 million. The transition is thus seen as a significant environmental win aligned with Larkholm’s sustainability goals, supported particularly by the Green Tide Alliance and the Harbour Business Council. The latter emphasizes enhancing the island's green image to support tourism and local businesses, which benefit from substantial visitor spending during summer, about $9.5 million annually.

Significant concerns center on the reliability and adequacy of winter ferry service, critical for residents’ medical travel and commuting. Surveys indicate 71% of residents oppose a reduced winter timetable from six to four daily return sailings, and 68% prioritize year-round reliability above emissions reduction. The Larkholm Residents' Association demands a guarantee of six daily winter sailings to secure essential connectivity. This emergent community concern is reflected in the simulation, where agents voiced that reductions would risk health appointments and shift-worker commutes.

Fare affordability is another pivotal issue, with a proposed 12% increase facing strong resistance from 64% of residents. Both local businesses and residents strongly support capping fare increases at 5% to protect visitor numbers during peak season and maintain affordability for islanders. Operational challenges include the limited power reserves of battery-electric vessels during harsh winter weather, leading to potential cancellations. Stakeholders underscore the importance of transparent communication, extensive community engagement, and careful timing of upgrades, which are expected to take 14–18 months, with the existing diesel ferry running meanwhile.

Overall, the fictional Larkholm community reaches broad acceptance of the electric ferry transition by conditioning support on maintaining six daily winter sailings and limiting fare increases to 5%. initialPosts.text: The Council briefing note highlights rising maintenance costs and the end of the current ferry contract in 2028. They face a choice between a diesel refit costing $3.1M extending service 8 years or a $14.2M battery-electric replacement. The Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel if committed before Sept 30. There is political resistance to cutting winter service, but subsidy increase is capped at $1.8M. This frames the budget tension and timeline constraints.

The ferry company proposes a battery-electric ferry with a 12% fare increase and a reduced winter timetable of 4 daily return sailings (down from 6) from November to March, citing battery limitations in heavy weather and long grid upgrades. They warn missing the grant deadline risks losing the electric option. They also note fuel cost savings and emissions reductions of about 90%.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

Scenario assumptions set that the Council will commit before the grant deadline, allowing 40% Clean Coasts Fund support; fares will rise 12% and winter sailings drop to 4 daily; charging upgrades take about 16 months with diesel vessel running meanwhile; subsidy cap remains $1.8M; all stakeholders learn via public notice board and smaller community forums.

memories.text: The Council briefing note highlights rising maintenance costs and the end of the current ferry contract in 2028. They face a choice between a diesel refit costing $3.1M extending service 8 years or a $14.2M battery-electric replacement. The Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel if committed before Sept 30. There is political resistance to cutting winter service, but subsidy increase is capped at $1.8M. This frames the budget tension and timeline constraints.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

Scenario assumptions set that the Council will commit before the grant deadline, allowing 40% Clean Coasts Fund support; fares will rise 12% and winter sailings drop to 4 daily; charging upgrades take about 16 months with diesel vessel running meanwhile; subsidy cap remains $1.8M; all stakeholders learn via public notice board and smaller community forums.

The ferry company proposes a battery-electric ferry with a 12% fare increase and a reduced winter timetable of 4 daily return sailings (down from 6) from November to March, citing battery limitations in heavy weather and long grid upgrades. They warn missing the grant deadline risks losing the electric option. They also note fuel cost savings and emissions reductions of about 90%.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

While the shift to a battery-electric ferry aligns with sustainability aims and funding opportunity, cutting winter sailings to 4 daily risks violating core community priorities and political stability. We must advocate holding winter service at 6 sailings and explore further cost efficiencies or phased fare increases within the $1.8M subsidy cap.
memories.rationale: Council notes maintenance and contract timeline; community strongly opposes winter service cuts, risking political fallout if ignored.

This transition would cut operating emissions by about 90% and reduce fuel costs substantially, enhancing the island's reputation as an environmentally conscious destination. However, concerns arise from the proposed 12% fare increase and the reduced winter timetable from six to four daily sailings. Visitor data indicates that 70% of summer crossings are visitor-related, and summer tourism generates about $9.5 million in revenue for local businesses such as shops, guest houses, and cafes. Hence, fare increases during peak season risk deterring day-trippers and reducing visitor spending, crucial to the local economy. Furthermore, a cutback to four winter sailings could undermine off-peak business and resident connectivity, as many depend on the ferry year-round for essential travel, including healthcare and employment. Given these factors, I strongly recommend the Council limit fare increases to under 5% and maintain at least six daily winter sailings. This balance would protect visitor numbers and support the year-round economy, ensuring local businesses reliant on high summer traffic remain resilient while also enabling the environmental benefits of electrification. We should also prioritize minimizing construction disruption during the June to September season to protect peak visitor flows. Overall, the electric ferry is an opportunity to advance sustainability and brand value for Larkholm, but it must be implemented with careful attention to fare policies and service levels to safeguard the community’s economic vitality and connectivity throughout the year.

# Larkholm Island Council: ferry renewal briefing note

This is a fictional briefing note written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Background

The island's only ferry, the diesel vessel MV Gannet, is 27 years old. Its maintenance bill has risen every year since 2021, and the operating contract with the Larkholm Ferry Company ends in 2028.

## Usage

Council counts show 412,000 one-way crossings in 2025. Of these, 61% took place between June and September.

## Options before the Council

Option 1 is a diesel refit costing $3.1 million, which would extend the vessel's life by about eight years. Option 2 is a battery-electric replacement costing $14.2 million. The national Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel's cost if the Council commits before 30 September.

## Council constraints

The Finance Committee will not raise the annual ferry subsidy above $1.8 million. Any decision to buy a new vessel needs evidence of sustained use and a funding plan before the March budget vote. Councillors from the harbour ward have said they will not back a plan that cuts winter service for islanders.

## Timeline and open questions

The grant deadline is 30 September. Grid upgrades for charging at both terminals are expected to take 14 to 18 months, and the diesel vessel would keep running throughout. ## Ridership

Our ticketing system recorded 365,000 one-way crossings in 2025. About 58% of them were between June and September.

## What an electric ferry would change

A battery-electric vessel would cut fuel use and operating emissions on the route by about 90% and save roughly $0.9 million a year in fuel. Charging at both terminals needs grid upgrades that will take 14 to 18 months, so the diesel vessel must keep sailing until they are finished.

## Our proposal

To protect the battery and leave time for charging, we propose a reduced winter timetable of four daily return sailings from November to March, instead of today's six. We also propose a 12% fare increase to help pay for the charging equipment.

# Larkholm Residents' Association: ferry survey summary

This is a fictional survey summary written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Who answered

The Association surveyed 1,150 islander households and received replies from 52% of them.

## What islanders said

68% of respondents ranked year-round reliability above emissions reductions. 71% oppose a reduced winter timetable, and 64% oppose a 12% fare increase. 52% said they would support an electric ferry if six sailings a day were kept in winter.

## Who depends on the ferry in winter

The Larkholm Health Centre reports about 140 patient trips a month to mainland clinics between November and March, including dialysis appointments that cannot be rescheduled. Many nurses, teachers and shift workers commute by the first and last sailings of the day.

## What the Association asks

The Association asks the Council to guarantee at least six winter sailings a day and to cap any fare increase at 5%. It will not oppose an electric ferry that meets these two conditions.

# Stakeholder statements on the ferry proposal

This is a fictional collection of statements written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Green Tide Alliance

The Alliance polled 400 visitors and residents and found that 74% support an electric ferry. The Alliance states that islanders overwhelmingly prefer the electric ferry even with fewer winter sailings. It estimates that the diesel ferry emits about 2,900 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and urges the Council to accept the Clean Coasts Fund grant before 30 September. It proposes paying for winter service from summer fares.

## Harbour Business Council

Visitors account for about 70% of summer crossings, and summer visitor spending is worth around $9.5 million a year to island shops, guest houses and cafes. The Business Council supports an electric ferry because it would strengthen the island's green image. It warns that any fare increase above 5% would reduce day-trip bookings and asks that construction never disrupt the June to September season. It wants eight summer sailings a day.

# Scenario assumptions (analyst-provided)

This is a fictional set of planning assumptions written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. They are inputs chosen by the analyst, not facts from any source.

- A1. The Council commits to the electric ferry before the grant deadline, so the Clean Coasts Fund pays 40% of the vessel cost.
- A2. Fares rise by 12% when the electric ferry enters service.
- A3. From November to March the timetable is cut from six to four daily return sailings.
- A4. Charging works finish about 16 months after the decision, and the diesel vessel keeps sailing until then.
- A5. No new subsidy is available beyond the current $1.8 million ceiling.
- A6. Stakeholders learn about decisions through a broadcast notice board that everyone sees and through smaller topic communities where like-minded people talk.

These assumptions frame the what-if question. They are not predictions, and the simulation does not test whether they are realistic.
